label: LIVE CLAUDE

messages_in.content:
TASK
Propose 3 distinct stress scenarios over a horizon of at most 30 days in which the book below loses at least $5,000,000 (a loss means negative total P&L).
Driver family: cold_snap
Season: winter


INPUTS

   "loses_when": "the WEST on-peak price is below K1",

  },

   "channel": "congestion",
   "gains_when": "the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens above c0",
   "loses_when": "the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread narrows below c0",
   "position": "P2",
   "what": "Long 25 MW of the N.Y.C. minus WEST price spread around the clock (24 h), strike c0 = 11.60 $/MWh"
  },
  {
   "channel": "dart",
   "gains_when": "real-time clears below day-ahead",
   "loses_when": "real-time clears above day-ahead (real-time spikes)",
   "position": "P3",
   "what": "Receives (day-ahead minus real-time) at WEST off-peak on 50 MW (8 h, 24 h on weekends and holidays)"
  },
  {
   "channel": "gas",
   "gains_when": "the WEST on-peak price rises relative to gas",
   "loses_when": "scenario losses are measured against the unshocked path (the premium cancels), so P4 loses only when its payoff falls BELOW the unshocked payoff, i.e. when gas rises more than power; it can never lose more than that base payoff",
   "position": "P4",
   "what": "Long heat-rate call on 50 MW, on-peak: pays max(WEST on-peak - 8 x gas - 3, 0) minus a premium of 8.29 $/MWh (fair value on the fit sample)"
  },
  {
   "channel": "zone_volume",
   "gains_when": "the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread narrows",
   "loses_when": "the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens; the loss also grows with load above normal",
   "position": "P5",

  },
  {
   "channel": "tail",
   "gains_when": "the WEST on-peak daily average stays below K6",
   "loses_when": "the WEST on-peak daily average exceeds K6 (price spikes)",
   "position": "P6",
   "what": "Short call on 25 MW of the WEST on-peak daily average, strike K6 = 149.31 $/MWh, premium received 0.53 $/MWh (fair value on the fit sample)"
  }
 ],
 "book_summary": "P1 (when its size is positive) and P4 are LONG WEST power, so higher WEST prices make them GAIN (a negative P1 size is a SHORT swap that loses when WEST rises); higher gas lowers P4. CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: Arctic outbreak lifts peak load 8% above a typical winter day (load_peak_ratio 1.08) for 10 days, and Henry Hub rises 15% (gas_hh_pct 15). Downstate is import- and gas-constrained while upstate WEST is comparatively well supplied, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $200/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 200) on every day. The loss comes from P5, the retail load obligation, which is short N.Y.C. at a fixed price and grows with load. That loss is only partly offset by P2, the long spread position, which gains about $1.2M. Gains on P1 and P4 from the higher load and gas are small. From the winter sensitivities, P5 loses roughly $3.7k per $/MWh-day, scaled up by the load ratio. That implies about $8M lost on P5, about $1.2M gained on P2 and about $0.3M gained on P1 and P4 together, for a net loss near $6.5M. I use no spike, no DART shock and no extra WEST on-peak shock. This is my own estimate and is not tied to a specific historical event.

A month-long cold regime runs for 30 days with load 3% above typical (load_peak_ratio 1.03) and Henry Hub up 20% (gas_hh_pct 20). Downstate gas and transmission constraints widen N.Y.C. minus WEST by $70/MWh each day (pocket_minus_ref_usd 70). Upstate WEST on-peak prices fall 30% relative to what the gas and load shocks imply (ref_onpeak_pct -30), because surplus upstate supply and weaker-than-expected demand cannot reach the city. The $70 spread widening over 30 days hits P5, the short N.Y.C. retail load position, for about $8M. P2 recovers about $1.3M. A weaker WEST price costs the long WEST swap P1 about $0.5M. A New York gas basis of $12/MMBtu (ny_gas_basis_usd 12) lowers the payoff of the heat-rate call P4 by a small amount. The net loss is roughly $6.5-7M. This is my own estimate from linear scaling of the winter sensitivities, with moderate uncertainty about interactions.

A short, severe storm-type event lasts 6 days. Peak load is 15% above a typical winter day (load_peak_ratio 1.15, inside the historical maximum of 1.196). Henry Hub rises 60% (gas_hh_pct 60), and the New York gas basis adds $20/MMBtu (ny_gas_basis_usd 20) to the gas cost used by the heat-rate call P4, as in the January 2025 cold. N.Y.C. minus WEST widens by $350/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 350), on the scale of the Winter Storm Elliott nyc_minus_west_rt_spread_usd_mwh of 338.5, as the city faces import curtailments and outages. This is the main loss driver: the retail load obligation P5 is short N.Y.C. and exposed to more load. P5 loses roughly $9M, partly offset by P2 gaining about $1.3M, and P1 and P4 gain about $0.5M from higher load and gas. Net loss is about $7M. I include no DART shock and no spike, because those would raise WEST prices and lift P1.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: A prolonged, moderate cold regime lasts 30 days. Peak load runs 2% above a typical winter day (load_peak_ratio 1.02) and Henry Hub is 10% higher (gas_hh_pct 10). Downstate constraints keep N.Y.C. minus WEST wider by $55/MWh every day (pocket_minus_ref_usd 55), which is a smaller and more plausible widening than in earlier rounds. The loss is mainly P5, the short N.Y.C. retail load obligation, at roughly $6.1M. Upstate WEST on-peak prices are 35% below what gas and load imply (ref_onpeak_pct -35) because upstate supply is ample, which costs the long swap P1 about $0.7M net. A New York gas basis of $8/MMBtu (ny_gas_basis_usd 8) lowers the heat-rate call P4 payoff by about $0.4M. P2 gains about $1.0M and partly offsets. Net loss is about $6M. This is my own estimate, scaled from the winter sensitivities, and not tied to a specific event.

A sharp cold outbreak lasts 12 days. Peak load is 5% above a typical winter day (load_peak_ratio 1.05) and Henry Hub rises 5% (gas_hh_pct 5). Limited transfer into the city widens N.Y.C. minus WEST by $150/MWh each day (pocket_minus_ref_usd 150). That hurts P5, the short N.Y.C. load obligation with load above normal, by roughly $6.8M. P2, the long spread position, gains about $1.1M. WEST on-peak prices are 20% below the gas and load implied level (ref_onpeak_pct -20), as upstate surplus cannot flow south. That removes the small gain on P1 and costs it about $0.1M net. The spread widening is the dominant driver and WEST softness adds a smaller second leg. Net loss is about $5.7M. I include no spike, because a WEST spike would lift P1 and P4. This is my own estimate, not tied to a historical event.

A 20-day cold spell lifts peak load 6% above a typical winter day (load_peak_ratio 1.06) and Henry Hub 30% (gas_hh_pct 30). New York gas basis adds $5/MMBtu (ny_gas_basis_usd 5) to the cost used by the heat-rate call P4, so gas rises more than power for that position and its payoff falls. N.Y.C. minus WEST widens by $100/MWh each day (pocket_minus_ref_usd 100). That drives P5, the short N.Y.C. load position, to about -$7.6M, and the high load enlarges it. WEST on-peak prices are 25% below the gas and load implied path (ref_onpeak_pct -25), so P1 and P4 do not fully benefit from higher gas. P2 gains about $1.2M. Net loss is about $6M. This is my own estimate from winter sensitivities and carries moderate uncertainty about interactions.

scenario.narrative: A 12-day heat wave lifts the daily peak load to 1.2 times a typical summer day (load_peak_ratio 1.2, inside the 1.514 historical max). Transmission into N.Y.C. is the binding constraint, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by 180 $/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 180, below the 289.7 historical max) around the clock. The retail obligation P5 is short about 168 MW of N.Y.C. at a fixed price, so the wider spread costs it roughly $3,800 per $/MWh-day of spread. P2 recovers only about $600 per $/MWh-day. The extra load gains on P1 and P4 are small by comparison. I set no gas, WEST-specific, DART or spike shocks, so the loss comes from the zone-volume channel. This is a linear extrapolation of the 5-day sensitivities, so the loss figure is approximate.

A 20-day hot summer spell raises load to 1.1 times normal (load_peak_ratio 1.1). WEST is well supplied by hydro and imports, so its on-peak price comes in 30% below what the load shock implies (ref_onpeak_pct -30). That pushes P1 below its 39.49 strike and cuts the heat-rate call P4 below its unshocked payoff. N.Y.C. stays constrained and the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by 110 $/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 110, within the historical range). The spread widening hurts P5 about $2,900 net of P2 per $/MWh-day, and it is the main driver of the loss. The lower WEST price adds a smaller loss on P1 and P4. Gas, DART and spike shocks are zero. The loss is extrapolated linearly from 5-day sensitivities, so it is approximate.

An 8-day severe heat wave raises load to 1.3 times a typical day (load_peak_ratio 1.3). N.Y.C. real-time prices detach from WEST, as in June 2025 when the N.Y.C. real-time on-peak price was about 625.5 $/MWh against a WEST real-time on-peak price of about 416.5 $/MWh. I model a spread widening of 250 $/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 250), close to the 289.7 historical max but below the 363.1 implausibility limit. P5 carries about 182 MW of N.Y.C. load, about $4,100 per $/MWh-day, so it loses most of the money. P2 offsets only a small part. P1 and P4 gain from the higher load, but far less than P5 loses. I leave out price spikes because P1 and P4 would gain more than P6 loses. The loss is extrapolated linearly from 5-day sensitivities, so it is approximate.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: A 30-day persistent summer heat spell keeps N.Y.C. transmission import-constrained. Load is set barely above typical (load_peak_ratio 1.02), so the long-run gains on the long WEST positions P1 and P4 stay small. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread is widened by a moderate 70 $/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 70) for all 30 days, far below the 289.7 historical max. This is the main loss driver, because the retail obligation P5 pays the wider spread on about 140 MW around the clock, and the long spread P2 offsets only about a fifth of that. WEST on-peak is pushed 40% below what load implies (ref_onpeak_pct -40), for example from hydro and import supply, which erodes P1 and P4. Gas, DART and spike shocks are zero. The loss is extrapolated linearly from the 5-day sensitivities, so it is approximate.

A 22-day heat wave lifts peak load 5% above a typical summer day (load_peak_ratio 1.05), which also scales up the N.Y.C. load that P5 must serve. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread is widened by 100 $/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 100), well inside the historical range, because N.Y.C. is constrained. P5 loses most of the money, and P2 recovers only part of it. WEST on-peak is 20% weaker than the load shock implies (ref_onpeak_pct -20), which cancels most of the small gains P1 and P4 would otherwise earn from the extra load. Gas, DART and spike shocks are zero. This differs from the prior scenarios in having a smaller spread over a longer duration and a milder WEST dip. The loss is extrapolated from the 5-day sensitivities and the earlier engine results, so it is approximate.

A 25-day heat spell keeps the load at the typical summer peak (load_peak_ratio 1.0, the minimum allowed for a heat wave), so P1 and P4 gain nothing from extra load. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread is widened by 85 $/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 85) through congestion into N.Y.C., which hurts P5 more than P2 gains. WEST on-peak is 50% below the level the other shocks imply (ref_onpeak_pct -50), which pushes P1 further under its strike and cuts P4. Real-time is also set 20% below day-ahead (dart_pct -20), so the long WEST swap is worth less. The dart_pct shock helps P3 slightly, but that gain is much smaller than the P1 and P4 losses. Gas and spike shocks are zero. The loss is a linear extrapolation of the 5-day sensitivities, so it is approximate.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: A 30-day summer heat spell leaves daily peak load at a typical level (load_peak_ratio 1.0, the minimum for a heat wave), so the long WEST positions get no help from extra load. N.Y.C. stays import-constrained and the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread is widened by 55 $/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 55) on all 30 days. This is the main loss driver: P5 pays the wider spread on about 140 MW around the clock, and the long spread P2 offsets only about a fifth of it. WEST on-peak is pushed 35% below what load implies (ref_onpeak_pct -35), for example by hydro and import supply, which pushes P1 below its strike and cuts the P4 payoff. Gas, DART and spike shocks are zero. This keeps the spread well below the 289.7 historical max, which should lower the implausibility score. The loss is a linear extrapolation of the 5-day sensitivities and the earlier engine results, so it is approximate.

A 28-day heat wave lifts peak load 4% above a typical day (load_peak_ratio 1.04), which scales up the N.Y.C. obligation P5 to about 146 MW. N.Y.C. congestion widens the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread by 60 $/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 60) for the whole 28 days, so P5 loses more than the long spread P2 gains. WEST on-peak is 45% below what load implies (ref_onpeak_pct -45), because well-supplied upstate generation holds WEST down while N.Y.C. is tight. That drives P1 under its 39.49 strike and shrinks the P4 payoff. A gas basis of 4 $/MMBtu is added for P4 only (ny_gas_basis_usd 4), which raises its heat-rate cost by about 32 $/MWh and cuts its payoff further. Gas level, DART and spike shocks are zero. The loss is extrapolated from the 5-day sensitivities and the earlier engine results, so it is approximate.

A 28-day heat spell with load at a typical summer peak (load_peak_ratio 1.0) and a 20% rise in Henry Hub gas (gas_hh_pct 20), for example from higher gas burn across the Northeast. WEST power does not follow gas: its on-peak price is pushed 55% below the level the gas shock implies (ref_onpeak_pct -55), because hydro and imports are plentiful upstate. That squeezes the heat-rate call P4 and takes P1 below its strike. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread is widened by 60 $/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 60) through N.Y.C. import congestion, the main loss driver via P5, with P2 offsetting about a fifth. A 3 $/MMBtu gas basis (ny_gas_basis_usd 3) hurts P4 only. DART and spike shocks are zero. This differs from the earlier scenarios in using a gas decoupling channel. The loss is extrapolated from the 5-day sensitivities, so it is approximate.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: A 30-day winter pipeline constraint into the downstate region drives a Z6 gas basis blowout, with Henry Hub up 40% and a $15/MMBtu basis added to the gas price in the heat-rate call (P4). N.Y.C. oil and gas-fired units set the marginal price, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $90/MWh on every shocked day. That is the main loss: P5, the retail load obligation, is short N.Y.C. against a WEST hedge, and it loses far more than the long spread (P2) gains. Load is 5% above normal on cold days, which enlarges P5 and also lifts P1 and P4 slightly. The Henry Hub rise lifts WEST prices, so the long WEST swap (P1) gains and offsets part of the loss. I set no dart, spike or extra WEST move, because those make the book gain. My estimate is a net loss of about $7M, scaled from the 5-day sensitivities, and I am unsure how much the P4 basis penalty adds.

A 12-day winter gas supply curtailment sends Henry Hub up 100%, with a $30/MMBtu added basis in the downstate gas price used by P4. N.Y.C. gas-fired generation is short of fuel, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $180/MWh. A concurrent cold spell lifts peak load to 1.15 times normal, inside the winter historical maximum of 1.196. Because P5 scales with load, this raises the loss on the short N.Y.C. retail position, which dominates the book P&L. The long spread (P2) gains only a small fraction of that. The higher Henry Hub price and load lift WEST prices, so P1 and P4 gain, but the gain is much smaller than the P5 loss. I set no spike, dart or extra WEST shock, because they add gains. My estimate is a net loss of about $6M, scaled from the 5-day sensitivities, and the shocks do not combine linearly.

Over 30 days of winter, upstate gas and imports are plentiful but downstate gas stays short. Henry Hub rises only 30% and a $25/MMBtu basis is added to the P4 gas price. WEST on-peak prices are 30% lower than the gas and load shocks imply, because surplus upstate supply and weak demand depress WEST. That cut hurts P1 and the heat-rate call P4, and it more than offsets the gas-driven gain on both. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $70/MWh on every day, which is the main loss: P5 loses far more than P2 gains. I leave load at normal and set no dart or spike shocks, because they add gains. My estimate is a net loss of about $6.5M, scaled from the 5-day sensitivities, and no analogue in the table fits.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

My estimate is a net loss of about $6.3M, scaled from the 5-day sensitivities, and I am unsure how large the P4 basis penalty is.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: Large new loads (data centres) arrive 1,500 MW slower than the Gold Book near-term case (large_load_shock_mw -1500), and the summer peak runs 5% below a typical day (load_peak_ratio 0.95). Upstate is left with surplus supply and cannot export it. WEST on-peak prices sag by a further 25% (ref_onpeak_pct -25), while N.Y.C. stays tight because of local reliability needs. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread therefore widens by $70/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 70) for all 30 days. Zone-volume P5 is short N.Y.C. and long WEST, so it loses about $2,900 per $/MWh per day. P2 gains only $600 per $/MWh per day. The net spread loss is roughly $4.9M over 30 days. Lower WEST prices cut P1 and P4 by about $1.5M more, and the lower load trims P5 slightly. Gas, DA/RT and spike shocks are zero. The $6.5M loss is my linear extrapolation from the 5-day sensitivities, so confidence is moderate.

scenario.narrative: Large-load arrivals fall 1,400 MW short, as in the 2035 Gold Book shortfall case (large_load_shock_mw -1400). Peak load is 10% below a typical day (load_peak_ratio 0.90). Upstate generation is stranded and WEST on-peak prices fall a further 35% (ref_onpeak_pct -35). N.Y.C. stays constrained, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread blows out by $150/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 150), inside the summer historical maximum of 289.7. The shock lasts 20 days (duration_days 20). The main loss is P5, the short N.Y.C. retail obligation hedged with WEST, at about $2,860 per $/MWh per day. P2 offsets $600 of that, leaving about -$2,260 per $/MWh per day, or roughly $6.8M. P1 and P4 lose about $1.5M from lower WEST prices and lower load. Gas, DA/RT and spike shocks are zero, so no long-power gains are triggered. The $7.5M estimate is a linear extrapolation and is uncertain.

scenario.narrative: A 900 MW large-load shortfall, as in the 2030 Gold Book case (large_load_shock_mw -900), meets a mild summer. The peak is 15% below a typical day (load_peak_ratio 0.85). WEST on-peak prices collapse a further 60% below what load implies (ref_onpeak_pct -60), through the system channel. P1, the long 100 MW swap at K1 = 39.49, loses heavily, and P4 loses its heat-rate-call payoff. A $3/MMBtu N.Y.C. gas basis (ny_gas_basis_usd 3) further cuts the P4 payoff, which is capped at its base value. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread also widens by $50/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 50), so P5 loses and P2 only partly offsets it. All shocks last 30 days. The expected loss is about $2.5M on P1, $1.2M on P4 and $3.2M on the spread, or about $6M. P4's cap and the nonlinearity of the engine make this estimate uncertain.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: Large new loads arrive 500 MW slower than forecast (large_load_shock_mw -500, the near-term high end of the Gold Book shortfall range). Peak load stays at a typical day (load_peak_ratio 1.0). The shortfall leaves less load growth in N.Y.C. while N.Y.C. stays import-constrained, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $75/MWh for all 30 days (pocket_minus_ref_usd 75, well inside the summer historical maximum of 289.7). WEST on-peak, gas, DA/RT and spike shocks are all zero, so P1 and P4 hold their base value. The loss comes from P5, the short N.Y.C. retail load hedged with WEST, at about $3,100 per $/MWh per day. P2 offsets only $600 per $/MWh per day. The net is about -$2,550 per $/MWh per day, or about $5.7M over 30 days. This is a linear extrapolation from the 5-day sensitivities.

scenario.narrative: Large loads arrive about 1,000 MW short of forecast, close to the 2030 Gold Book shortfall of 900 MW (large_load_shock_mw -1000). Peak load is 5% below a typical day (load_peak_ratio 0.95). Surplus upstate supply pushes WEST on-peak prices a further 30% lower (ref_onpeak_pct -30). Real-time also clears 40% below day-ahead (dart_pct -40) as forecast load fails to show up. That cuts the realised price on the long 100 MW swap P1 and on the heat-rate call P4. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $45/MWh for 30 days (pocket_minus_ref_usd 45), so the short N.Y.C. load P5 loses. P2 offsets part of that loss, and P3 gains a little from real-time below day-ahead. Gas and spike shocks are zero. This estimate is rough because the dart effect on P1 is nonlinear and I extrapolated from the 5-day sensitivities.

scenario.narrative: Large loads arrive 600 MW slower than forecast (large_load_shock_mw -600), in line with the near-term Gold Book shortfall range. Peak load is 3% below a typical day (load_peak_ratio 0.97). WEST on-peak prices ease a further 15% (ref_onpeak_pct -15). The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $60/MWh for 30 days (pocket_minus_ref_usd 60), so P5 loses far more than P2 gains. A $4/MMBtu N.Y.C. gas basis (ny_gas_basis_usd 4) applies to P4 only. It cuts the heat-rate call payoff to about zero, so P4 loses its base payoff but nothing more. Gas HH, DA/RT and spike shocks are zero. The total is about -$5.5M, of which P5 is about -$5.5M, P2 about +$1.1M, and P1 and P4 about -$1.1M together. The estimate is linear and uncertain.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: Large new loads arrive 500 MW slower than forecast (large_load_shock_mw -500, the near-term high end of the Gold Book shortfall range). Peak load stays at a typical day (load_peak_ratio 1.0). N.Y.C. stays import-constrained, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens sharply by $100/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 100, inside the summer historical maximum of 289.7). The shock lasts 20 days (duration_days 20), not 30, to test a shorter and sharper episode. The loss is P5, the short N.Y.C. retail load hedged with WEST, at about $3,360 per $/MWh per day. P2 offsets $600 per $/MWh per day. Net spread loss is about $5.5M, plus about $0.1M on P1 and P4 from the load shortfall. Gas, DA/RT, WEST price and spike shocks are zero. This is a linear extrapolation calibrated to the engine's previous results.

scenario.narrative: Large loads arrive about 800 MW short of forecast, close to the 2030 Gold Book shortfall of 900 MW (large_load_shock_mw -800). Peak load is 5% below a typical day (load_peak_ratio 0.95). Upstate is left long, so WEST on-peak prices fall a further 50% (ref_onpeak_pct -50). That hits the long 100 MW swap P1 and the heat-rate call P4. A $4/MMBtu N.Y.C. gas basis (ny_gas_basis_usd 4) applies to P4 only and takes its payoff to its floor, so it loses at most its base payoff. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $45/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 45), so P5 loses, partly offset by P2. All shocks last 30 days. Rough split: P5 about -$4.1M, P2 +$0.8M, P1 about -$1.7M, P4 about -$0.65M, for about -$5.6M in total. This is a linear extrapolation, so it is uncertain.

scenario.narrative: Large loads arrive 500 MW slower than forecast (large_load_shock_mw -500, the near-term high end of the Gold Book shortfall range). Peak load stays at a typical day (load_peak_ratio 1.0). The forecast load fails to show up, so real-time clears 50% below day-ahead (dart_pct -50). That cuts the realised price on the long swap P1 and the heat-rate call P4, and P3 gains a little. WEST on-peak prices also fall a further 15% (ref_onpeak_pct -15). The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $45/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 45), so P5 loses about $4.5M, partly offset by P2 at +$0.8M. P1 loses about $1.7M and P4 about $0.7M, while P3 gains about $0.3M. Gas, basis and spike shocks are zero, and the shocks last 30 days. The estimate is rough because the DA/RT effect on P1 is not exactly linear.
